demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making eye contact with other people
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
The event happened because of the way I acted
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Uniform or Weapons' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another unless there is additional unreported trauma involving military, police, or armed threat. It introduces a highly specific cue set not supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I have to be on guard all the time' and the threat item 'I need to stay alert' imply ongoing external danger surveillance. For a guilt-based accident trauma, this is possible but, alongside the rest of the profile, it pulls toward a current-threat/assault formulation rather than the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: These vigilance-focused items cluster around danger-monitoring, whereas the memory and appraisal content otherwise fit grief/guilt and disorganization after causing injury. That mismatch is clinically harder to explain than ordinary heterogeneity.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on guilt, grief, and fragmented memory after accidentally causing serious injury, which is coherent, but the anger/rage theme is not well integrated with the rest of the formulation. Fear of losing control of anger plus irritability/aggressive behavior suggests a prominent violence/rage presentation that is not otherwise reflected in the memory content, appraisals, or strategies tied to this trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
issues.explanation: Compulsive exercise appears poorly connected to the rest of the selected items. The other maladaptive strategies are avoidance-based and directly related to interpersonal shame or medical reminders, whereas excessive exercise implies a separate regulation strategy that is not supported by the rest of the profile or the specified edge pattern.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively
issues.explanation: Given the active formulation, Memory and Threat should be tightly linked. The memory items emphasize fragmentation and grief, while the threat items are limited to nonspecific arousal symptoms (concentration, irritability, sleep) rather than a trauma-linked sense of current threat. This makes the irritability/anger strand especially weakly anchored in the stated cognitive formulation.

The Threat node is dominated by generic arousal/distress items (concentration and sleep problems) rather than a sense of current threat linked to the trauma. Given the formulation, Threat is strongly driven by memory and negative appraisals, so threat items should more clearly reflect ongoing danger, guilt-based threat, or feared consequences connected to having seriously injured someone.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
issues.explanation: 'Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore' is a broad depressive/existential appraisal that is not well anchored to this trauma profile. The other appraisal items are specifically guilt/responsibility based (self-blame, failed to protect), which fit the trauma type and the strong Negative Appraisals → Threat edge; this item pulls the node toward a different syndrome and weakens internal coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
issues.explanation: Avoiding eye contact is hard to connect specifically to accidentally causing serious injury to another unless there are accompanying appraisals about others judging or condemning her. No such interpersonal-judgment threat/appraisal is represented elsewhere, so this strategy is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Anna is a 35-year-old married White American woman who works as a counselor, and when she first began describing the accident in therapy, what stood out was not a single clear account but a series of broken images she could not comfortably join together. She could tell there had been an ordinary day, a drive, a moment when another person was badly hurt because of something she had done, but when she tried to say it aloud the memory came in jagged pieces: the sudden movement, the impact, a glimpse of the other person on the ground, sound without sequence, then a blankness she could not bridge. Each time she circled back to it, she was overcome not only by shock but by grief so intense that she would stop speaking and stare at the floor, as if continuing would make the scene more real. What tormented her most was that she felt she should be able to explain exactly what happened and could not. Even to herself, the story would not hold together.

In the weeks after the accident, Anna became certain that the injury had happened because of the way she had acted. She did not describe it as bad luck or a tragic mistake. In her mind it was simpler and harsher: she had failed, and another person had paid for that failure. She had come to believe that she should have protected others and that she had done the opposite. Those thoughts settled into something broader and heavier. The work she had once experienced as purposeful-sitting with clients, helping them make sense of pain-began to feel hollow. She kept going through the motions, but privately she felt that nothing in her life carried meaning in the same way anymore. She would come home to her husband and feel the distance between who she had been and who she now believed herself to be.

At work, these changes showed up in small but noticeable ways. Anna had always been known as warm and attentive, someone whose steady presence put people at ease. After the accident, she found herself avoiding eye contact with clients and colleagues. Looking directly at another person felt unbearable, as if their gaze might contain accusation or expectation she could not meet. In sessions she sometimes fixed her attention on her notes or on a point over the client's shoulder. She knew this made her seem less present, and that awareness brought another layer of shame. She did not explain the change. She simply tried to get through the day without having to feel seen.

She also began organizing her life around avoiding anything medical. The sight of an ambulance on the road could send a jolt through her body and leave her gripping the steering wheel, heart racing, scanning the scene as if something terrible were about to happen again. Hospitals became impossible. Even routine physical examinations were put off. She told herself she did not need them yet, that she was too busy, but underneath was a visceral dread of corridors, gurneys, monitors, and the whole world of injury and emergency care that brought her too close to what she could not bear to remember. If she heard sirens while driving to the counseling center, she sometimes detoured or sat in the parking lot longer before going inside, trying to settle herself.

Anna spent a great deal of effort trying not to think about the accident. The harder she pushed the images away, the more she seemed to live in readiness for their return. Nights became especially difficult. Sleep no longer came easily; she lay awake braced against thoughts she did not want, or woke and could not settle again. During the day she felt on guard, watchful in a way that was exhausting and hard to explain. Her body seemed to anticipate danger even in ordinary settings. Strong feelings were never far away-fear, horror, anger, guilt, shame-and she moved through them with the sense that any reminder could tip her back into the rawness of the event.

By the time she sought help, the strain had become difficult to hide at home and at work. Her husband had noticed that she seemed absent even when she was sitting beside him, and that she recoiled from conversations that asked for honesty about how she was doing. At the counseling center, avoiding eye contact and carrying herself in a tense, guarded way had begun to affect how connected she felt to her clients. What finally brought her in was not a single crisis but the realization that she could no longer tell herself this would pass if she just kept suppressing it. She wanted, at minimum, to be able to sleep and to tell a coherent story of what had happened. What frightened her most was that if she looked directly at the memory-or let other people look directly at her-she would only confirm what she already believed: that she had failed someone in the worst possible way, and that nothing meaningful could be built from that.
